Imagination machine · test case 01 · updated 22 Oct 2026

Paper Warrior Studies

Can one Midjourney image become a game-ready model that is faithfully the same object, not just "inspired by" it? This test case is a folded-paper Roman legionary, taken through three rounds and broken into parts. Every pass is rendered from the reference camera, scored against the image, and logged.

Where it stands: the silhouette, camera, pose and light match well, and round 2 made the figure read as paper rather than clay. It is still a close cousin of the reference, not the same model. A person notices four gaps first: the shield is a flat slab, the crest goes dark from behind, the skirt is thin strips instead of wide tabs, and the face plate is weak (it now has its own study). The props show that the parts approach works, and that each part needs a second round. Round 3 showed that a turnaround sheet fixes shape errors no single view can catch, which makes it the most valuable input so far.

Round 1 · 22 Oct, morning

Fit the image

Judged loss 0.469 → 0.267Silhouette IoU 71% → 85%3 LODs · 1,449 / 3,510 / 8,060 trisStatus done

The first question was whether a loop could pull one exact model out of one picture. I wrote one parametric builder for an armoured humanoid, defined a loss against the image, and let an optimizer and three Claude models revise it. It found the pose, camera and light. It did not find the style: the surface came out as noise instead of folds. Round 2 is about that.

The loss

Every candidate is built by a Blender script from about 200 numbers, then scored against the reference at 256 px. The loss has five parts, each 0 when perfect:

0.35 × (1 − IoU) + 2.0 × outline distance + 0.2 × (1 − SSIM) + 0.2 × (1 − facet-edge correlation) + 0.6 × colour error

The silhouette comes from my own cut-out of your image. I fitted the teal backdrop as a smooth gradient and kept the pixels that differ from it, with a separate rule for the floor so the cast shadow doesn't count as the warrior. The quick inner loop scores only the silhouette, about 10 evaluations a second. Full scoring needs a Cycles render and takes 2 to 9 seconds.

The silhouette fit

Two attempts by the numeric optimizer, each fitting the camera, then the pose, then the shapes. Attempt A started with the body turned the way my first guess said, and it settled at 0.100. I looked at the render, saw that the crest was edge-on and the stance was mirrored, and restarted with the body turned the other way. Attempt B reached 0.069. No amount of tuning carried A across that gap on its own.

Attempt A, body yaw −12°Attempt B, body yaw +30°Ticks mark camera → pose → shape stages

Milestones, judged on the same settings

Each stage re-rendered at 512 px, LOD1, 32 samples, so the numbers compare fairly. Top row is the render. Bottom row is the silhouette overlay: white matches, blue is where the reference has warrior and the model doesn't, red is the reverse.

The fidelity dial

The same loop with three bundles. Each run starts from the camera-fitted template and gets 6 rounds. In each round the model sees the reference, the current render and the overlay, plus the loss history, and proposes parameter edits. An edit is kept only if the loss drops. Mid and high also run a numeric polish after each round. I ran every bundle twice: once with the plain prompt (v1), and once with a coarse-to-fine prompt I wrote after watching v1 fail (v2). Revisers ran through the Claude Code CLI, and cost is the CLI's own reported spend.

The asset

Three detail levels exported as GLB, each one mesh in one material: 1,449, 3,510 and 8,060 triangles. They're in the project files with provenance.json and the parameters that rebuild them. The turntable spins the figure under the fitted light. The back was never seen, so the back is a guess.

Critique

What I built, and why it looks like this

I didn't ask a model to write Blender code from scratch every round. I wrote one parametric builder for an armoured humanoid. The body is a metaball skeleton that gets decimated into flat facets. The helmet, crest, skirt strips, shoulder flaps, sash, greaves and shield are procedural paper pieces. That choice made the loop fast and the loss smooth enough to optimise, because every candidate is one JSON file. It also capped fidelity from the first minute. The loop can only reach shapes the builder can express. The reference's Corinthian-style face plate, its layered lorica tabs and its brushy crest aren't fully in the vocabulary, so no amount of revising could produce them.

What moved the loss, and what didn't

Three of my own moves account for most of the drop. Restarting with the body turned the other way took the judged loss from 0.428 to 0.315. Fitting the lights, exposure and backdrop colour took it to 0.279. The final Opus pass took it to 0.267. In the dial runs, the language-model edits themselves were the smaller lever. Across the Sonnet and Opus runs, the model's accepted edits cut the loss by 0.007 to 0.037, and the numeric polish after each round cut it by 0.053 to 0.083. Haiku had no polish and earned all of its 0.04 itself, for three cents. Per dollar, the cheapest model was by far the most efficient reviser.

The detail pass is the clearest case of the loss not caring. Pectorals, abdominal plates, a nose, fingers, greaves, a raised sash, cheek guards, a wider crest and denser facets made the render visibly more like the reference, and the loss moved from 0.2794 to 0.2788. At 256 px those details are a few pixels each, and the silhouette and tone terms swamp them.

Where the loss disagreed with my eye

Fat limbs. When the pose was wrong, the silhouette optimizer covered the missing area by thickening arms and legs. The overlap went up and the warrior turned into a linebacker. Some of that bulk is still in the final torso.

Facing. After the restart, the silhouette matched well while the figure read as if seen from behind, because the helmet showed no face and the chest showed no sash. A silhouette can't tell front from back. Opus caught this in round 3 of the master run, in its own words: "the render reads as seen from behind or in rear three-quarter: no visor or face shows". It turned the body from 30° to 18°, which also lowered the loss. That was the only global correction any reviser made.

Paper versus clay. The best-scoring model, at 0.267, has strong per-vertex crumple. On the turntable it looks like wet clay or rock. Paper is a few large flat planes with crisp creases, not noise. I cut the crumple and the facet count for the final asset, and the loss rose to 0.278, because the facet-edge term rewards any high-frequency edges, real folds or not. I shipped the version that looks like paper and scores worse. That term needs replacing before it can be trusted.

Shiny paper and camera height. The lighting fit chose a glossier paper (roughness 0.44) because gloss bought contrast, and the reference is matte. The camera height wandered between 0.7 m and 1.6 m across fits with almost no change in loss, because a silhouette barely constrains it.

What each dial setting got wrong

Haiku, low. It read the overlay precisely. It quoted pixel offsets, made five or six small edits a round, and got four or five of six accepted. It never looked past the overlay to ask whether the figure faced the right way, so it polished a wrong pose. It's good value for local cleanup and can't be trusted with the big picture.

Sonnet, mid. With v1 it bundled eight to ten edits a round, and four of six rounds were rejected. In round 5 it noticed the problem itself ("rounds 2 to 4 failed because they changed too many things at once"). With the v2 prompt it made smaller moves and finished best of all the dial runs, at 0.355 judged, for $0.40. Most of that gain came from the numeric polish it was paired with.

Opus, high. It gave the best diagnoses. It isolated variables on purpose ("this round only moves the shield, to test that change"), and it made the one global fix. It also cost about $0.15 to $0.35 a round, and in the dial runs most of its improvement came from the polish, not its edits. With the v2 prompt it finished at 0.383, worse than its own v1 run at 0.375 and worse than Sonnet v2. These are single runs, so the ordering of Sonnet and Opus here is within run-to-run noise, and I wouldn't rank them from it.

What I said I'd change next, and what round 2 did about it

  1. Start from several hypotheses.done in round 2 The biggest win was a restart I did by eye. Try a small grid of body turns, mirror flips and camera heights at the start, fit each one cheaply, and keep the best. That's minutes of compute and no model calls.
  2. Spend the expensive model where judgement matters.open Use Opus once at the start for the global read (facing, camera, proportions, which parts exist) and once at the end as the critic. Run Haiku plus the numeric optimizer for the many local rounds in between. That should beat Opus every round for a fraction of the cost.
  3. Let the high setting change structure, not just numbers.open The real ceiling was the builder's vocabulary. At high fidelity the model should be allowed to write new parts into the script, such as a face plate, layered tabs or a brush crest, and have each one scored like any other edit.
  4. Fix the loss.part crops and style term in round 2 Add high-resolution crops for the head, hands and shield. Replace the edge term with something that sees folds rather than noise; a perceptual feature metric would be the obvious choice, but its weights couldn't be downloaded in this container. Add a model-judged "does it read right" term covering facing, a visible face and the paper material.
  5. More than one view.needs the Mac One image leaves the back invented. A Midjourney turnaround sheet (front, side, back) would give three targets, and that's where Midjourney on your Mac pays off. Connect that Mac with Remote Control and the loop can request sheets itself.
  6. Repeat runs before ranking models.open Each bundle ran once per prompt, so model quality and luck can't be separated yet. A fair dial comparison needs three or more runs of each.

Recommended dial settings for the next asset

SettingWhat runsExpected costGood for
DraftMulti-start numeric fit, then Haiku × 6, LOD0≈ $0.03, 3 minBlocking out a prop or creature fast
StandardMulti-start, Opus global read once, Haiku or Sonnet rounds with numeric polish≈ $0.40–0.60, 5 minMost game assets

Round 2 · 22 Oct, afternoon · after Evan's feedback

Keep the style

Judged loss v2 0.447 → 0.306Winner C, hybridStatus done, with known gaps

What you asked for

Your read of round 1 was that the geometry was good but the art style didn't survive. Three things carry the look:

  • The silhouette of the crest, shoulders, shield and skirt matters more than any small detail.
  • The surface has to be deliberate folds and overlapping plates, not arbitrary triangles.
  • Art direction is not polygon reduction. Fewer triangles does not make paper.

The bigger point was about architecture. Don't reconstruct the finished model; reconstruct the rules. That means a papercraft construction grammar that could turn any asset into this style, from a knight to a London street. A shader can't fake a folded silhouette, so the rules have to make geometry. You asked for three competing experiments (geometry-first, procedural papercraft and a hybrid) and bet on the hybrid.

You also asked whether the mesh is generated from scratch or optimised from an existing one. It is generated: every piece is Python in Blender, with no third-party mesh anywhere.

What changed in the machine

A loss that looks where you look. Loss v2 keeps the whole-figure terms and adds 512 px crops of the five parts you named (crest and helmet, shoulders, shield, skirt, legs and feet). Each crop is scored on overlap and structure. It also adds a style term that compares the distribution of edge strength and edge coherence inside the figure. Folded paper is mostly flat planes with a tail of strong, straight creases. Crumple noise is lots of medium, incoherent edges. That term lets the loss tell paper from clay, which round 1's edge term couldn't.

A grammar instead of a model. paper.py holds style rules that run on any mesh, whatever it depicts:

RuleWhat it doesApplied to
facetRe-triangulates to a target edge length, then crumples by a fraction of the local edge, so the paper reads the same at any scale or detail levelBody skin, trim
bandsCuts the surface with straight, tilted planes, splits it along the cuts and lifts alternate bands, so armour reads as overlapping paper strips with clean seamsTorso armour
platesClusters faces into plates, flattens each one, folds a ridge down its middle and overlaps them like shinglesTried on the torso, then switched off (see below)
stiffenGives sheet parts paper thickness and a slight hand-made twist per pieceSkirt tabs, shoulder flaps
materialMatte paper: high roughness, a faint sheen and a tiny fibre bump. No fake folds in the shader.Everything

Three experiments

A, geometry-first: refit the plain builder with the part-crop loss and no grammar. B, procedural papercraft: keep round 1's geometry and run it through the grammar. C, hybrid: A's refitted geometry, then B's grammar. All three were judged on the same settings: loss v2, LOD2, 512 px, 48 samples.

VersionJudged totalWhole silhouetteCrestShouldersShieldSkirtLegsStyle
Round 1 final0.4470.14884%88%88%93%72%0.49
A · geometry-first0.3650.10586%93%92%96%83%0.35
B · papercraft grammar0.3190.17283%87%86%91%70%0.09
C · hybrid0.3060.11085%94%92%95%81%0.19

Lower is better for the total, the whole silhouette (1 − IoU) and style. The part columns are silhouette overlap inside each crop, where higher is better.

The numbers say what you predicted. Geometry alone fixes the silhouette but not the look. The grammar alone fixes the look and scores by far the most paper-like, but it sits on round 1's lumpier geometry, so it loses on every part crop. The hybrid keeps nearly all of A's silhouette and most of B's style, and wins overall.

Critique of round 2

What worked

Separating style from shape was the right cut. Once the grammar was its own module, the style term could reward it independently of the silhouette, and the two could be combined without refitting. The part crops did what they were meant to. The shoulders went from 88% to 94% and the legs from 72% to 81%, changes a whole-figure loss had been too coarse to notice.

What didn't

Clustered plates. My first plate rule grouped faces with k-means and folded each group. The groups follow the triangulation, so the seams came out ragged and stair-stepped, the opposite of a deliberate fold. I replaced it with straight-seam bands. Those are clean, but too subtle at this lift: from the reference camera they barely show.

The shield. It is still a thick slab with a rim. The reference shield is one smooth, curved oval sheet with crisp edge facets. The builder has no single-curved-sheet primitive, so no amount of fitting can reach it.

The crest. It's built from two layers of blades, and from behind the inner faces fall into shadow, so it reads as a dark brush. The reference crest is light from every side.

The skirt. It's many thin strips, where the reference has fewer, wider tabs that overlap. That's as much a parameter-range problem as a builder one.

The loss still prefers some crumple. Even with the style term, the best-scoring version carries more surface noise than I'd ship. The style term measures edge statistics, not whether the edges line up into folds. It judges better than round 1's term, but it isn't the final judge.

What I learned

A style is a set of construction rules plus a vocabulary of primitives, and the primitives set the ceiling. The grammar can only make the shapes it is allowed to make: a curved sheet, a wide tab, a single-layer crest. The cheapest next win is adding those primitives, not more optimisation. That's also why splitting the character into parts is the right next move: each part needs only a small, specific vocabulary.

Round 3 · 22 Oct, evening · Midjourney turnaround

Three views

All-view silhouette loss 0.237 → 0.107Rendered, all views 0.375 → 0.281Status done

Round 1 ended with "one image leaves the back invented." A Midjourney turnaround sheet gave three targets of one figure: front, left side and back. It's a new design in the same paper style, not the original warrior. It's stockier, stands straight, carries a round-oval shield and a short sword, and has a transverse brush crest. So this round tests a different question: what does a second and third view buy?

Two caveats from the sheet itself. The views aren't true orthographic, and the side view is turned a little toward the camera. The fit is allowed to find that turn: it settled at 64° instead of 90°.

The experiment

Two fits from the same start (round 2's hybrid, reset to a neutral standing pose), with the same budget of about 3,000 evaluations and the same stages: camera, a shield-turn sweep, pose, proportions, parts, then everything. Front-only sees only the front view. Three-view scores the mean of all three. Every candidate in both fits is scored on all three views and logged, so the front-only fit can be judged on views it never saw.

Adding views is cheap. The figure is built once per candidate, and each view only re-aims the camera and rasters a silhouette. Both fits took about 12½ minutes.

Silhouette loss (lower is better)FrontSideBackAll three
Start (neutral pose)0.2240.3730.2260.274
Front-only fit0.1050.4070.1980.237
Three-view fit0.1210.0940.1060.107

The front-only fit overfits to its one view. It scores best on the front, and its side view ends up worse than where it started (0.373 to 0.407). From the front a shield is just an outline, and turning it to 122° matched that outline. From the side, that same shield sticks out in front of the body like a tray. Depth, the shield's turn and the crest's direction are all invisible from one view, so the optimizer was free to get them wrong.

The three-view fit gives up a little on the front to get everything else right. It's 15% worse on the front view (0.121 against 0.105) and more than twice as good overall. The shield turned to 69° and sits on the left arm, facing out, as in the sheet. The camera search also found the side view's real turn by itself.

Rendered and lit

Light, paper and backdrop were fitted on all three views at once (16 rounds of three renders each). The front-only model was rendered under the same light, so the comparison is about shape, not lighting.

Rendered judged lossFrontSideBackMean
Start0.3850.5030.3660.418
Front-only, lit0.2900.4920.3430.375
Three-view, lit0.3070.2590.2760.281

Same terms as the props: silhouette, outline distance, structure (SSIM), colour and the style term, scored per view.

Critique of round 3

What multi-view changed

It fixed the class of error that cost the most in round 1. The biggest single gain in round 1 was a facing restart I had to make by eye. Here the side and back views settle facing, shield placement and depth by themselves, with no restart and no model call. That makes the turnaround sheet the most valuable input so far. It beats a better optimizer and it beats a more expensive reviser, because it removes a guess instead of searching harder around it.

What it didn't change

The look. The renders still show round 2's vocabulary on a new design: thin skirt strips, a crumpled body, and a smooth helmet where the target has a hinged face mask and brow ridge. The structure and style terms barely moved between the two fits (0.264 against 0.266, 0.165 against 0.173), because more views only constrain shape. The style gap is still a primitives gap: lorica bands, wide pteruges, a round shield with a raised rim and a sword all need builder parts that don't exist yet.

Things that aren't in the model at all. The target has a sword and a scaled apron in front. The builder has neither, so both stay blue in every overlay, and the optimizer leans the hand out to cover the sword. That's the same "fat limbs" failure as round 1, at a smaller scale.

The sheet isn't perfectly consistent. Midjourney draws the crest thinner from the back than from the side, and the side view is turned. The fit absorbs the turn as a camera angle, but it can't satisfy a crest that changes size between views. Some of the remaining side and back loss is the target disagreeing with itself.

What I'd do next

Make the turnaround the default input for the machine: front, side and back, plus a three-quarter view when the design has an asymmetric part like a shield. Weight the views by how much each one can see. Then spend effort on the primitives the look needs. Geometry is now pinned down well enough that style is the bottleneck.

Offshoots · 22 Oct, late afternoon

Parts and kit

Helmet own study, in progressProps 5 fitted twiceComposed first passKit body + 6 socketed partsStatus in progress

Your idea was piecemeal design: supply simpler props and make the character composable. Each part gets its own builder in the same paper grammar, its own reference image and loss, and a socket on the body. The helmet became a separate study because the face plate is the hardest single piece.

Helmet study

This is running separately, against your helmet image, with the face plate as the focus. Its results will be added here when it's done.

Five props, two fits each

Each prop has its own builder:

  • Cuirass: lorica hoops with chest plates and layered shoulder guards.
  • Pauldrons: rimmed arches stacked on each other.
  • Belt: a band with a buckle frame.
  • Sandals: a sole with crossing straps.
  • Greaves: faceted shells.

The fit is round 2's recipe in miniature. It tries three camera turns, fits camera and shape on the silhouette for 300 steps, then fits light and paper over 20 renders. Every step goes into the same loss log, about 3,200 evaluations over both fits.

The second fit kept the camera inside a sensible range for each prop, switched to cream paper, rebuilt the pauldrons as three nested domes, and thinned the sandal straps. All five scores went down.

PropFit 1Fit 2Read by eye after fit 2
Greaves0.2050.200Closest. The shape and facet size are right. The back plate's edge doesn't show, and the colour should be cream.
Cuirass0.2920.277Good outline and hoops. The chest plates split at the centre and the shoulder guards are too flat. The reference hoops are deeper and more stepped.
Sandals0.2980.279Right layout, but the soles are too thick and the straps too chunky and crumpled. The reference straps are clean, smooth loops.
Belt0.3140.310The ring is right, but it's too thin and tilted. The buckle is an H instead of a rectangle with a tongue, and the tail doesn't show.
Pauldrons0.3170.291Biggest change. Now three nested domes, as in the reference, but one cap still drifts away from its pair, and the domes are too flat at the crown.

What the props taught me

Small, specific builders fit fast: each prop took about six minutes with no model calls. Where the builder's vocabulary matches the object, as with the greaves and the cuirass, one pass gets close. Where it doesn't, as with the pauldrons' nested domes and the belt's buckle, the optimizer makes up for it by moving the camera. That's round 1's lesson again at a smaller scale. Two fixes follow. First, lock the camera to a sensible range for each prop. Second, use Opus once per prop to read the reference and choose the builder's structure before any fitting, the "spend the expensive model on judgement" idea from round 1.

Cream paper helped the tone score on every prop, but the gains in the second fit are small (0.004 to 0.026). Most of what is left is structure, not tuning: the belt needs a real buckle and tongue, the cuirass a closed front, and the sandal straps smooth loops. Those are builder changes.

The composed warrior

Each second-fit prop is rebuilt and snapped onto the hybrid body. The body's own shoulder flaps and leg bands come off, and the props replace them. A prop isn't sized from the joints alone. It's sized to wrap the actual body mesh: the cuirass to the torso's cross-section, the greaves to the shin's radius, the sandals to the foot. Each prop is also exported as its own GLB with its origin at its socket.

Honest read: the mechanics work. Every part lands on its socket, and the cuirass hoops, the belt and the greaves read clearly. It doesn't look better than the one-piece hybrid yet. The body underneath is still the bulky round-1 mesh, so the props sit on a figure that's too thick. The pauldrons come out small, and the sandals mostly disappear into the feet. The fix is to slim the body into a mannequin that the parts dress, instead of armour layered over armour.

The socketed kit

The hybrid warrior is also exported as a kit. It has a body with named socket points (head, chest, waist, hands, shoulders, back, feet) and one GLB per part. Each part's origin sits at its socket, and every part is listed in kit.json with a hash. The props will snap onto these sockets next.

Next

  1. A slim mannequin body for the parts to dress, then refit the composed figure against the original image as one score.
  2. Builder fixes per prop: a buckle with a tongue, a closed cuirass front, smooth sandal loops and domed pauldron crowns. Then add the helmet once its study lands.
  3. New primitives in the grammar: a single curved sheet for the shield, wide overlapping tabs for the skirt, and a single-layer crest that stays light from behind.

Provenance

This applies to every round. All code, parameters, GLBs and logs are in the abbiesworld_ios repo under tools/paper-warrior.
